clue.text: Scared of a ragged sound

indicators.note: Sound asks for the noise the words in front of it make, not the letters they are spelt with.

blocks.note: a ragged cuff is a frayed one, and the little article in front joins the sound rather than sitting apart from it

explanation.surface: Somebody frightened by a rough, tattered noise.
explanation.walkthrough: The noise is the trap: the line reads as a sound somebody is scared of, and that word is the instruction to listen instead. Frayed and ragged both describe cloth coming apart at the edge.
explanation.definitionFit: To be afraid is to be scared — afraid of the dark, scared of the dark — the same adjective either way round.

clue.text: Stable pet almost a cert

blocks.note: a stable government or a stable ladder is a firm one
a pet subject or the teacher's pet is the favourite one

explanation.surface: A horse kept in the yard that looks a near-certain winner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stable' looks like the building the pet lives in and is the adjective meaning steady. A cert is British slang for a certainty, and it belongs to the racing page, which is what keeps the horses in view.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm favourite is the one everything is expected to go to — the horse or the film the money is on — which stops just short of a certainty.

clue.text: Therapist has an article on a composer, reportedly

indicators.note: In a down entry what sits on something rests above it, so the piece named first goes in at the top.
Reportedly asks for the name as it is said out loud, not as it is written.

blocks.note: the clue names an indefinite article and hands over the very word it used
the other indefinite article, a single letter of it
Liszt, the Hungarian who wrote the Hungarian Rhapsodies, has a name said as 'list'

explanation.surface: A therapist who has written a piece about a composer, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' is the piece of writing in the surface and the grammarian's a-or-an in the wordplay, which is how two tiny words slip past. Foreign names are fair game for a sound clue as long as the English pronunciation is the common one.
explanation.definitionFit: An analyst here is the psychoanalyst — somebody in analysis goes to see their analyst — so therapist names the same practitioner by trade.

clue.text: Split to separate the German Rolling Stone?

indicators.note: To separate something is to force its parts apart, so the word named after it opens in the middle and takes the other piece into the gap.

blocks.note: der is one of the German words for 'the'
a split between friends or within a party is a rift

explanation.surface: A break-up that parts a German member of the Rolling Stones.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital letters make Rolling Stone look like the band, and the definition is the proverb about the stone that gathers no moss. German words for 'the' — der, die, das — are standing crossword furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: A rolling stone is the one who never settles anywhere, which is exactly what a drifter does, moving from town to town and job to job.

clue.text: French woman gets first man to interrupt me

indicators.note: To interrupt is to cut in part-way through, so the piece named before it lands inside the word that follows instead of beside it.

blocks.note: the setter speaking, the two letters exactly as written
Adam is the first man in Genesis

explanation.surface: A Frenchwoman setting the first man on earth to cut across what I am saying.
explanation.walkthrough: Everything hangs on a two-letter word: 'me' is the setter, and the rest of the wordplay goes inside it. Madame is the form of address for a married Frenchwoman, where mademoiselle is the unmarried one.
explanation.definitionFit: Madame is what a French woman is called to her face, and English borrows the word for the woman herself.

clue.text: Good for mother to hide hot fluid

indicators.note: To hide something is to cover it over, so the word doing the hiding closes round the letter named before it.

blocks.note: mama is the nursery word for mother
G is the short form of good, the grade on a school report

explanation.surface: A mother covering up something scalding for everybody's good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good for mother' reads as one domestic phrase, the sort a family says, and the two halves are on opposite sides of the wordplay. The stuff keeps this name only while it is underground; once it reaches the surface it is lava.
explanation.definitionFit: Magma is the molten rock beneath the Earth's crust, so hot fluid names it by what it physically is rather than by what geologists call it.

clue.text: Goes out with sticky food

blocks.note: what one person does with another they are seeing regularly
the sweet brown fruit of the palm, sold pressed into a block

explanation.surface: Somebody going out in the company of a sticky snack.
explanation.walkthrough: The two halves run into one sentence with no join at all, which is the shape a double definition always takes. The fruit arrives squashed into a slab, so the second half describes it as much as it names it.
explanation.definitionFit: To date somebody is to go out with them, and a date is the sticky fruit of the date palm — one set of five letters for both.

clue.text: Crunch point at half-time?

blocks.note: read as the tense moment of a match, and meant as the crisis itself, the point where something has to give
read as the interval between the halves, and meant as the halfway mark of a life rather than a game

explanation.surface: The tense moment in a dressing room with a match half gone.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here comes apart into letters: the clue works by letting half-time mean a football interval on the surface and half a life underneath. What it names is the sports car and the sudden new haircut at fifty.
explanation.definitionFit: A midlife crisis is the panic that arrives halfway through a life, so the whole clue describes it — a crunch point reached at the halfway mark.

clue.text: Slowing down when conserving energy – smashing!

indicators.note: To conserve something is to keep hold of it inside, so the word doing the conserving closes round the letter named after it.

blocks.note: a car slowing down is braking
E is the physicist's symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A driver easing off to save fuel, and what a splendid thing that is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smashing' is the British word for splendid, which is why the clue ends on a cheer; the answer wants it for broken crockery instead. Conserving energy is exactly what a driver slowing down is doing, so the instruction disappears into the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: To break something is to smash it — breaking a window, smashing a window — so the two present participles swap straight over.

clue.text: Alter backward current

indicators.note: Something backward runs the other way about, so the word in front of it goes into the grid from its last letter.

blocks.note: to alter a text is to edit it, and those four letters are entered the other way round

explanation.surface: Changing a current that is behind the times.
explanation.walkthrough: Three words and four letters leave nowhere to hide, so the only question is which word is the definition. 'Current' is the sea's rather than the electrician's, and this is the one current that turns round twice a day.
explanation.definitionFit: The tide is the twice-daily flow of water in and out along a coast, so current names it by the movement it is.

clue.text: Dubious moment, non-starter

indicators.note: A non-starter never gets going, so the word beside it loses the letter it starts with.

blocks.note: a jiffy is a moment — back in a jiffy

explanation.surface: A doubtful moment for a plan that was never going to work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Non-starter' reads as the hopeless scheme and is the instruction to drop a first letter. A jiffy is informal British for the shortest imaginable stretch of time.
explanation.definitionFit: Something iffy is doubtful and not to be relied on — an iffy excuse, an iffy connection — which is what dubious means.

clue.text: Send first of many in conveyance

indicators.note: First of asks for the opening letter of the word that follows and nothing else of it.
In puts the letter just taken inside the word named after it rather than alongside.

blocks.note: goods in transit are goods being conveyed from one place to another
the letter that word begins with

explanation.surface: Sending the first of many parcels off in a van.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First of many' is a toast, and only the M of it is wanted. Transit is the state of being carried rather than the thing doing the carrying, which is what makes conveyance fit it.
explanation.definitionFit: To transmit something is to send it out — a station transmits, a disease is transmitted — so send is the everyday verb for it.

clue.text: Cassava tarnished beholden image

indicators.note: Beholden means held by something — bound to it by a favour — and what is held stands unbroken inside the words in front of it.

blocks.note: the run starts near the end of the first word and carries straight on into the second

explanation.surface: A crop gone off, and the picture somebody is obliged for.
explanation.walkthrough: Cassava is the starchy tropical root that tapioca is made from, and it is in the clue only for the letters at its end. The join between the two words is where the answer straddles, which is what makes it hard to see.
explanation.definitionFit: An avatar is the picture standing in for a person on a screen, so image names it by what appears — in Hindu belief, a god's bodily form.

clue.text: Shore bird took wing, heading off after mutt

indicators.note: A heading sits at the top, and heading off takes the first letter away from the word in front of it.
After sends what has just been described behind the piece named next, so the dog goes in first.

blocks.note: a cur is a mongrel dog, the word a Victorian villain spits
a bird that took wing flew, and the instruction beside it lifts the f off the front

explanation.surface: A bird by the water that flew off the moment a dog appeared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Took wing, heading off' reads as one continuous flight, and the comma is the only sign that a letter goes missing. The curlew is the long curve-billed wader whose call carries across an estuary at dusk.
explanation.definitionFit: The curlew feeds on estuary mud and tideline, so shore bird places it by habitat rather than naming its family.

clue.text: Get up in heart of funeral procession

indicators.note: In a down entry what goes up is read from the bottom end, so the word before it is written in backwards.
In drops the piece already in hand inside the word named after it instead of beside it.

blocks.note: the heart of an apple or of a problem is its core
the plainest verb in the language, entered from the bottom up as the instruction beside it asks

explanation.surface: Standing up in the middle of a funeral procession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get up in' reads as rising from a seat and is carrying three separate jobs. A cortège is the slow line of cars behind a hearse, French by origin and printed in English without its accent.
explanation.definitionFit: A cortège is the train of mourners and vehicles following a hearse, which is a funeral procession named straight.

clue.text: Snake on an old train

blocks.note: the rattlesnake, named for the dry buzz of horn at the end of its tail
a train that shakes and bangs along the track, and American slang for a freight train hoboes rode

explanation.surface: A snake travelling on an ancient train.
explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions with one small word between them is the whole clue, and that word is there to make the sentence work rather than to move anything. Both senses come from the same noise: the tail's buzz and the carriages banging over the rail joints.
explanation.definitionFit: A rattler is the rattlesnake, and a rattler is also a clattering old train — both named from the sound they make.

clue.text: Rebellious person, in the main

blocks.note: somebody who refuses to obey the people set over them
read as 'for the most part', and meant as 'at sea' — the main is the old word for the open ocean

explanation.surface: Somebody who is rebellious most of the time.
explanation.walkthrough: No letters change hands: the clue defines a rebel and then quietly says where to find this particular one. The main is the open sea, as in the Spanish Main, and rebellion afloat has always had its own name.
explanation.definitionFit: A mutineer is a crew member who rises against the ship's officers, so the rebellion is the definition and the water is what narrows it to one word.

clue.text: Find examples within contents list

indicators.note: Within says the letters wanted are already sitting inside the words beside it, unbroken and in the order they stand.

blocks.note: the run begins one letter into the first word and crosses the gap into the second

explanation.surface: Looking for instances inside a table of contents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Find' reads as the instruction to go looking and is part of the hiding place instead. An index is the alphabetical list at the back of a book, where the table of contents sits at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: An index lists what a book holds and where each thing is, so contents list names it by the job it does.

clue.text: Outing the very large overall character

indicators.note: An outing takes a thing out of its usual place, and letters taken out of theirs come back in a different order.

blocks.note: the three letters of 'the' and the OS stitched into very large clothing — five letters to be re-sorted

explanation.surface: Exposing the larger-than-life character of somebody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outing' reads as the tabloid sense, the public exposure of a private fact, and does the shuffling. OS is the size label on outsize clothes, which is how two letters come to mean very large.
explanation.definitionFit: The ethos of a school or a firm is the character running through the whole of it, which is what an overall character means.

clue.text: Grow weary of American covering

blocks.note: what the legs do on a long walk, and what a listener does during a long story
the rubber round a wheel, spelt the American way where British English writes tyre

explanation.surface: Growing weary of the coverage coming out of America.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half turns entirely on spelling: the rubber is a tyre in Britain and drops its y across the Atlantic. 'Of' is the only join and it belongs to the first half.
explanation.definitionFit: To tire is to grow weary, and in American spelling a tire is the rubber covering on a wheel.

clue.text: Society heard to give expensive coat

indicators.note: Heard asks for the sound the word in front of it makes rather than the way it is spelt.

blocks.note: a guild is the old society of craftsmen who controlled a trade in a town, and said aloud it can be spelt without the u

explanation.surface: A society reported to be handing out costly coats.
explanation.walkthrough: The goldsmiths had a guild of their own, so the sound and the sense of this clue sit unusually close together. Only the crossing letters settle which of the two spellings the grid wants.
explanation.definitionFit: To gild something is to lay a thin skin of gold over it, which is about the most expensive coat anything can be given.

clue.text: That chap's around Leeds, unexpectedly incautious

indicators.note: Around sends the words before it right round the outside, leaving the rest to sit in the middle.
What happens unexpectedly comes out in an order nobody planned, and so do these letters.

blocks.note: that chap is he, and the 's makes two letters that come apart to let the rest in
the five letters of the Yorkshire city, standing in a new order

explanation.surface: A fellow wandering round Leeds without a care in the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That chap's' has to be heard as two letters plus an s, and the apostrophe is exactly where the wordplay opens up. Leeds is the West Yorkshire city, here for its letters alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody heedless pays no heed to what is going on around them, which is what being incautious amounts to.

clue.text: Former king returned by small Persian king

indicators.note: What is returned comes back the way it went, so the words before it are read from their last letter to their first.

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner and rex is Latin for king, the title printed after a British monarch's name on a coin; the five letters go in from the far end
S is the size on a clothing label

explanation.surface: An old monarch brought back by a small Persian ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: There are two kings in the clue and only the second belongs to the definition; the first is the Latin title crosswords keep in stock. Xerxes ruled Persia in the fifth century BC and had the Hellespont whipped when a storm wrecked his bridge of boats.
explanation.definitionFit: Xerxes was the Achaemenid ruler who invaded Greece in 480 BC, so the definition names him by throne and country — one example of the kind.

clue.text: Lapse without opening or exit

indicators.note: Without says something goes missing and opening says which part: the letter the word starts with.

blocks.note: to lapse back into an old habit is to regress

explanation.surface: A failure with no way in and no way out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening or exit' reads as a matching pair of doorways, and the first of the two is an instruction rather than a noun. Egress is the formal word an architect or a fire officer uses for a way out.
explanation.definitionFit: Egress is the going out, or the means of it — a building must provide a means of egress — so exit says the same thing in everyday English.
